S033.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
S033.description: A distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood.

subtypes.Elevated Mood: A mood that is abnormally high, euphoric, and full of unmotivated happiness and vitality.
subtypes.Irritable Mood: A state where one gets angry or aggressive even at minor stimuli.
subtypes.Mood Lability: Rapid shifts in mood, alternating unpredictably between euphoria and irritability.

S034.name: Increased_Activity
S034.description: Abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy.

subtypes.Increased Energy: Overflowing physical and mental energy, leading to an inability to stay still and a desire to keep moving.
subtypes.Hyperactivity: Doing far more work than usual or starting multiple activities simultaneously.
subtypes.Psychomotor Agitation: Inability to tolerate resting or stopping, driven by a constant need to do something.

S037.name: Pressured_Speech
S037.description: More talkative than usual or pressure to keep talking.

subtypes.Talkativeness: Speaking far more than usual and continuing to talk without rest.
subtypes.Rapid Speech: Speech speed is so fast that it is difficult for others to understand or interrupt.
subtypes.Pressured Speech: Cannot stop talking or tolerate silence due to an internal pressure to keep speaking.

S039.name: Manic_Distractibility
S039.description: Attention is too easily drawn to unimportant or irrelevant external stimuli.

subtypes.Responsiveness to Extraneous Stimuli: Attention is immediately drawn to trivial and unimportant stimuli nearby (e.g., noise, movement).
subtypes.Frequent Task Switching: Unable to finish one task and constantly shifting attention to new things, starting multiple tasks simultaneously.
subtypes.Inability to Sustain Attention: Unable to focus on any activity for long, with attention constantly being scattered.

S040.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
S040.description: Increase in goal-directed activity (at work, school, socially, or sexually) or purposeless psychomotor agitation.

subtypes.Occupational Hyperactivity: Driving significantly more projects or work than usual in the workplace or academic setting.
subtypes.Social Hyperactivity: Becoming much more sociable and extroverted than usual, actively meeting and contacting people.
subtypes.Hypersexuality: Significantly increased interest in or activity regarding sex.
subtypes.Psychomotor Agitation: Purposeless non-goal-directed activity, such as pacing or hand-wringing, driven by an inability to sit still.

S041.name: Painful_Consequence_Behavior
S041.description: Excessive involvement in activities that have a high potential for painful consequences.

subtypes.Unrestrained Buying Sprees: Spending excessive amounts of money or shopping recklessly to a degree that creates financial distress for self and family.
subtypes.Foolish Business Investments: Making rash business investments or ventures without sufficient review.
subtypes.Sexual Indiscretions: Engaging in indiscriminate or risky sexual behavior that is out of character.
subtypes.Impulsive Risky Behavior: Excessively dangerous or foolish behavior, such as reckless driving or drug use, without considering the consequences.

symptom.disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder is characterized by at least one lifetime manic episode, typically lasting at least one week (or requiring hospitalization), often accompanied by marked impairment in social or occupational functioning. Manic episodes involve a distinct period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood and increased energy or activity, frequently associated with inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, impulsive behavior, and engagement in high-risk activities. Many patients also experience major depressive episodes over the course of illness, and the condition often follows a recurrent, episodic pattern with inter-episode recovery that can be incomplete. It is distinguished from Bipolar II Disorder by the presence of full mania rather than hypomania, and from primary psychotic disorders by the prominent mood component and episodic nature.

patient.personality: Paulyn is a routine-oriented, community-minded planner who enjoys keeping things orderly while fostering fun, cooperative activities with friends and neighbors.
patient.stressor: After leaving her barista job with the plan to "finally get serious" about finding an administrative assistant position, Paulyn suddenly had unstructured time and a strong desire to prove to herself and her family that she could build an adult life quickly. She began mapping out an ambitious schedule that included intensive job searching, organizing multiple community events, leading extra volunteer shifts, and starting new fitness and hobby projects all at once. Over the course of a month, what began as a focused transition plan escalated into a relentless drive to initiate new groups, committees, and social gatherings, crowding out sleep, basic self-care, and any downtime, and making it impossible for her to follow through consistently on job applications. Her parents encouraged her to seek psychiatric help when they noticed she was constantly launching new plans, talking about grand projects for the community while neglecting bills and household responsibilities, and becoming distressed when anyone suggested she slow down or prioritize.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’ve thrown myself into so many projects and plans lately that I can’t seem to stop starting new things, even though it’s getting in the way of actually getting a job.”

S033.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
S033.description: A distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood.
S033.manifestation: All month I’ve been either way up, buzzing with this almost giddy excitement about my ideas for the neighborhood, or snapping at my parents over tiny things like them asking about the electric bill, and I can feel myself flip from one extreme to the other in the same afternoon.

S034.name: Increased_Activity
S034.description: Abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy.
S034.manifestation: I wake up after just a few hours of sleep and feel like I’ve been shot out of a cannon, rushing around the house making lists, rearranging my room, planning events, and I just can’t sit still long enough to, say, quietly fill out a job application.

S037.name: Pressured_Speech
S037.description: More talkative than usual or pressure to keep talking.
S037.manifestation: When I start talking about my plans—like the job search, then the community potluck, then the walking group—I go so fast and jump from one to the next that people have to interrupt me to get a word in, and even then I feel this pressure in my chest to keep going.

S039.name: Manic_Distractibility
S039.description: Attention is too easily drawn to unimportant or irrelevant external stimuli.
S039.manifestation: I’ll be halfway through an online job application and suddenly I’m pulled away by a text about a bake sale or a random idea about repainting the community room, and before I know it I’ve opened five new tabs or started another project and never finished the form.

S040.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
S040.description: Increase in goal-directed activity (at work, school, socially, or sexually) or purposeless psychomotor agitation.
S040.manifestation: Instead of just focusing on finding an office job like I planned, I’ve signed myself up to run extra volunteer shifts, start a new neighborhood game night, organize a fitness challenge, and help with three different committees, and I’m constantly pacing or tidying when I’m home because I feel like I always have to be doing something.

S041.name: Painful_Consequence_Behavior
S041.description: Excessive involvement in activities that have a high potential for painful consequences.
S041.manifestation: I’ve been saying yes to everything—putting nonrefundable deposits down for event spaces, buying supplies on my credit card, offering free childcare for neighbors I barely know, and even riding with a friend who drives way too fast—without really thinking about how I’m going to pay for it or keep myself safe.
